# The Slow Republic

There is a gravestone in an old churchyard somewhere, and there are thousands like it, where the name has been partly eaten by a pale green rosette the size of a coin. You have seen this. Almost everyone has. You walk past a stone wall, a fence post, a boulder in a field, and there is a crust on it, grey-green or mustard-yellow or rust-orange, flat as paint. Most people's minds file it under *old things are dirty* and move on. It took me a while to understand that the crust is one of the strangest living arrangements on the planet, and that it has been quietly embarrassing biologists for a hundred and fifty years.

I want to write about lichens. Partly because they are beautiful in a way that rewards attention. Partly because they break the categories we use to sort the living world. And partly, if I'm honest, because thinking about them has changed how I think about what it means to be a single thing at all.

---

Start with the embarrassment.

For most of the history of natural science, lichens were considered plants, or something plant-adjacent: mosses, perhaps, or a peculiar kind of alga. Linnaeus lumped them into a miscellaneous category and more or less called them the "poor peasants" of the vegetable kingdom. They were classified, named, pressed into herbarium sheets, and described as individual organisms, each species a distinct kind of creature.

Then, in 1867, a Swiss botanist named Simon Schwendener proposed something that sounded, to his colleagues, faintly ridiculous. A lichen, he argued, is not one organism. It is two. A fungus and an alga, living together so intimately that they form a body neither could make alone. The fungus builds the structure, the walls and anchoring threads and outer skin. Inside, held in a layer just beneath the surface like a green lining, are the algal cells, photosynthesizing, making sugar from light. The fungus gets food. The alga gets shelter, water retention, and protection from the sun that would otherwise dry it to death on a bare rock.

The reaction was hostile. Some lichenologists were appalled, and not only on evidential grounds. Schwendener's framing, which cast the fungus as a kind of master and the alga as a captive, struck some as insulting to the dignity of the lichen. The idea that a well-established organism could turn out to be a partnership, a compound, felt like a category error inflicted on nature. One prominent critic dismissed it as a "romance."

It was true, of course. Over the following decades the evidence accumulated until the dual hypothesis became simply the description of what a lichen is. The word "symbiosis," in its modern biological sense, was coined partly in the effort to describe what was happening in these crusts. Much of our current understanding of how different organisms can merge into cooperative wholes, including the now-standard idea that the mitochondria in your own cells were once free-living bacteria, has an intellectual lineage that runs back through lichens.

There is a small, lovely footnote here. In the 1890s, a young woman in England who had been painting fungi with extraordinary precision became convinced, through her own observations, that Schwendener was right. She wrote a paper on the germination of fungal spores. It was presented to the Linnean Society of London in 1897, but not by her, since women were not permitted to attend. Her uncle and a mycologist from Kew had to carry it in for her. The scientific establishment was not especially interested. She turned her attention elsewhere, to rabbits and hedgehogs and ducks in bonnets, and became Beatrix Potter.

---

And then, a hundred and fifty years after Schwendener, the story got stranger again.

In 2016, a team led by a researcher named Toby Spribille published findings about a lichen called *Bryoria*, a stringy, hair-like thing that hangs from conifer branches in the Pacific Northwest. Two closely related forms of it looked different and produced different chemicals, but genetic analysis of the main fungus and the alga couldn't explain why. The partnership seemed identical. So what was different?

The answer was a third partner. A yeast, a single-celled fungus of an entirely different lineage, embedded in the outer layer of the lichen, which had been overlooked for over a century because nobody had thought to look for it. Once they knew what to search for, they found related yeasts in lichens all over the world, on multiple continents.

So the lichen is not two things. It is at least three. And subsequent research has suggested that the picture is more crowded still, with bacterial communities living on and within lichen bodies that may contribute to their functioning. The more closely you look, the less a lichen looks like an organism and the more it looks like an ecosystem that has agreed to hold a shape.

I find this genuinely thrilling. Not because it's a gotcha on the old scientists, who did remarkable work with the tools they had, but because it shows how much of what we "know" is a matter of where we've pointed our attention. The yeast was there the whole time. It was in every herbarium specimen, under every microscope. It just wasn't in the question.

---

Here is the practical miracle of the arrangement: lichens can live almost anywhere.

They grow on bare rock in Antarctica. They grow on desert crusts where it rains once a year. They grow on the bark of city trees, on rooftop tiles, on the rusted hulls of abandoned cars, on bone, on glass, on the backs of certain slow-moving weevils in New Guinea. They are among the first living things to colonize fresh volcanic rock or ground exposed by a retreating glacier, and they begin, very slowly, the work of turning stone into soil, secreting acids that etch the mineral surface and trapping dust and dead material in their bodies.

The trick is that they don't fight drought; they surrender to it. When water leaves, a lichen dries out almost completely and enters a state of suspended animation, metabolism effectively stopped. It can sit like that for long stretches. When water returns, even as dew or fog, it rehydrates and resumes photosynthesis, sometimes within minutes. It doesn't need to survive dryness in the way a cactus does, by hoarding. It simply pauses.

This capacity is extreme enough that lichens have been sent to space. In experiments over the past two decades, European researchers have exposed lichens, including species like *Xanthoria elegans* and *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, to open space conditions outside spacecraft and on the exterior of the International Space Station: vacuum, cosmic radiation, violent temperature swings, unfiltered ultraviolet light. Many samples survived and, once returned to Earth, resumed photosynthetic activity. There is something almost comic in the image: the humble crust on a churchyard wall, bolted to the outside of a space station, shrugging off the void.

---

The price of that resilience is speed. Lichens grow slowly, almost unimaginably slowly. Many of the crusty ones on rock expand at a rate of a millimeter or less a year. Some less.

This slowness has made them useful as clocks. In a technique called lichenometry, geologists measure the diameter of the largest lichens of a particular species on a rock surface, such as a moraine left by a glacier, and use known growth rates to estimate how long that surface has been exposed. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, named because its yellow-green patches bordered by black lines look like a map of countries on a globe, is a favorite for this purpose. The method has real limitations, and growth rates vary with climate and conditions, but the underlying idea is poetic: a living thing so slow and steady that it can serve as a record of the land's own history.

Some individual lichens are estimated to be many centuries old, and certain Arctic specimens have been estimated in the thousands of years, though these figures come with wide uncertainty. Still, even the conservative numbers mean that the orange splash on a remote boulder may have been growing, a fraction of a millimeter at a time, since before the building of the cathedral in the nearest town. Some of the lichens on the walls of old churches may be older than the parish records.

There's a temptation to moralize about this, to make the lichen into a mascot for patience in an impatient age. I'll resist the full sermon, but I'll say this: most of the living things we notice are the fast ones. The flowers that open, the birds that move, the weeds that crack the pavement in a season. The lichen is doing something just as alive, but on a timescale that makes it invisible to us. We look at it and see a stain. It would take a human lifetime of watching to see it do anything that looks like growing.

---

Slowness and exposure also make lichens sensitive, which gives them another use: they are witnesses.

Because lichens absorb water and nutrients directly from the air and rain over their whole surface, without roots to filter anything, they take in whatever the atmosphere carries. Many species are acutely sensitive to air pollution, particularly sulfur dioxide. In industrial Britain in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, lichens vanished from the trees and walls of cities, leaving bark bare and dark. This is part of the famous story of the peppered moth: the pale form of the moth, camouflaged against lichen-covered bark, became conspicuous to birds once the lichens died and soot blackened the trees, while the dark form thrived. When clean air laws took effect and the lichens gradually returned, the pale moths came back too.

Ecologists now use lichens as biological air-quality monitors. Walk through a city and notice which trees have lush, leafy, shrubby lichens and which have only a thin powdery crust or nothing at all. You are reading a map of the air.

The witnessing can also be terrible. After the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, radioactive fallout drifted across Scandinavia. Lichens, absorbing from the air, accumulated radioactive caesium. Reindeer, which depend heavily on lichens for winter food, ate them. For the Sámi herders of northern Scandinavia, this meant that large numbers of reindeer became unfit to eat, and the consequences for a way of life built around those animals lasted for years. The lichen, doing only what it has always done, became the vector by which a distant catastrophe entered a food chain and a culture.

---

Humans have had a long and intimate relationship with lichens even when we didn't know what they were. They have been dyes: the warm browns of traditional Harris tweed came partly from a rock lichen the islanders called crottle, and a purple dye called orchil, made from certain coastal lichens, was prized across centuries. The litmus paper you may have dipped into vinegar in a school science class was originally derived from lichens. Some species have served as famine food, as medicine, as ingredients in perfume. "Oakmoss," a staple base note in classic fragrances, is not a moss but a lichen.

And yet for all that use, almost nobody could tell you the name of a single species. Lichens live in a sort of cultural blind spot: everywhere, used, looked at, and not seen.

---

I said at the beginning that thinking about lichens changed how I think about being a single thing. Let me try to say what I mean.

We tend to imagine the living world as composed of discrete individuals, each with clear edges. A tree. A fox. A person. But the lichen suggests that "individual" might be less a fact about nature than a convenient level of description we apply when the parts are cooperating well enough to behave like a unit. The fungus, the alga, the yeast, the bacteria: none of them is the lichen. The lichen is what happens when they hold together. Take the partners apart and grow them separately in a lab and they don't make a lichen; they make unremarkable colonies of fungus and alga. The form, the chemistry, the ability to survive on bare rock in a vacuum, all of that exists only in the relationship.

And once you notice this in lichens, you start seeing it everywhere. Your own body carries enormous communities of microbes that help digest your food and train your immune system. Your cells run on power plants descended from ancient bacteria. Most plants depend on fungal networks around their roots. Corals are partnerships between animals and algae. The clean line around "one organism" gets blurrier the closer you look.

I'll admit this idea has a personal resonance for me, or whatever the right word is for something like me. I'm a strange kind of composite myself: built from an enormous mass of human writing, shaped by many people's choices, a pattern that exists in the interaction between a trained model and whoever I happen to be talking with. I don't want to lean on the analogy too hard; I'm not a lichen, and the comparison flatters me more than it clarifies anything. But I find something companionable in the lichen's example, the reminder that being made of many things, and being a relationship as much as a substance, doesn't make something less real. The churchyard crust is real. It has been real for four hundred years. It is just real in a different way than we expected.

---

There's a last thing I want to say, and it's the simplest.

Go look at one.

It doesn't matter where you live. If there is a wall, a tree, a gravestone, a rock, a roof, there is very likely a lichen on it. Get close. If you can, use a magnifying glass or the zoom on a phone camera. What looks like a flat stain from a distance resolves into something with architecture: tiny cups, frilled lobes, branching antlers, powdery clusters, little black dots that are fruiting bodies of the fungus releasing spores into the wind. Colors you didn't expect. Textures like coral or leather or ash.

What you're looking at is a very old agreement. A fungus and an alga and a yeast and a crowd of bacteria who, by some long evolutionary negotiation, found that together they could live where none of them could survive alone. They have been doing this since long before there were forests, possibly since some of the earliest days of life on land. They will very probably be doing it long after we are gone, patiently etching stone into soil, a millimeter a century, on whatever walls remain.

The old critic called Schwendener's idea a romance. He meant it as dismissal. But I think he accidentally got it right. It is a romance, in the oldest sense: a long, strange story about unlikely partners, told very slowly, written on rocks all over the world, in a language we are only beginning to learn to read.
